questions.stem: Old English grew out of the dialects of which peoples, who settled in Britain from the fifth century?
questions.explanation: Germanic tribes from what is now northern Germany and Denmark brought the dialects that became Old English. The Normans came much later, in 1066, and their French influenced Middle English.

questions.stem: Which set of everyday words entered English from Old Norse?
questions.explanation: Viking settlement in the Danelaw brought close contact between Old English and Old Norse, and basic words, even the pronoun ‘they’, were borrowed. ‘Court’, ‘jury’ and ‘judge’ came from Norman French.

questions.stem: Old English and Old Norse shared many word roots but had different inflectional endings. Many linguists argue that contact between their speakers contributed to:
options: the raising of long vowels in the Great Vowel Shift
the fixing of English spelling by the first printers
the loss of many inflectional endings in English
the arrival of French legal vocabulary in English
questions.explanation: When speakers shared roots but not endings, the endings carried less of the meaning, which is thought to have helped them wear away in northern English. French legal vocabulary arrived with the Normans, a separate incursion.

questions.stem: In English, ‘cow’, ‘pig’ and ‘sheep’ name the live animals, while ‘beef’, ‘pork’ and ‘mutton’ name their meat. This pattern is usually traced to:
options: the Latin brought to England by Christian missionaries
the spellings chosen by printers in the fifteenth century
the Norman French spoken by the ruling class who ate the meat
the Old Norse spoken by the Viking settlers living in the Danelaw
questions.explanation: After 1066, English-speaking peasants raised the animals while French-speaking nobles dined on the meat, so the French words were used for the food. The animal names are native Old English words.

questions.stem: Words of government and law such as ‘court’, ‘judge’, ‘jury’ and ‘parliament’ came into English mainly from:
questions.explanation: For about three centuries after 1066, law and government in England were conducted in French or Latin, so much legal vocabulary is French. Old Norse gave everyday words such as ‘sky’ and ‘egg’ instead.

questions.stem: After St Augustine's mission arrived in 597, Old English borrowed words such as ‘altar’, ‘priest’ and ‘candle’ from:
questions.explanation: Christian missionaries brought Latin as the language of the Church, and religious and learned vocabulary entered Old English. Norman French arrived nearly five centuries later.

questions.stem: Common expressions such as ‘a law unto themselves’ and ‘the powers that be’ trace back to:
options: Caxton's printed editions of Chaucer in the fifteenth century
English Bible translations, notably the King James Version of 1611
Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language, published in 1755
the legal documents of Norman French courts after 1066
questions.explanation: Bible translations by Tyndale and the 1611 King James Version were read aloud in churches for centuries, and many of their phrases became idioms. Johnson's Dictionary recorded and defined words rather than creating phrases like these.

questions.stem: After the Black Death of 1348–49, labour shortages raised the status of English-speaking workers. Historians of English link this period with:
options: English replacing French in law, schooling and public life
a wave of Old Norse borrowings into everyday English
the arrival of the printing press in England
Johnson's dictionary fixing the spelling of English words
questions.explanation: In the decades after the plague, English became the language of schooling and, from 1362, of pleading in the law courts, displacing French. Printing did not reach England until 1476.

questions.stem: William Caxton set up the first printing press in England, at Westminster, in:
questions.explanation: Caxton's press began printing in 1476, and his choice of mainly London forms helped spread one written standard. 1755 is the year of Johnson's Dictionary.

questions.stem: The printing press contributed to the standardisation of English mainly because:
options: it was used at first only to print dictionaries and grammar books
printers settled on spellings and spread them in many identical copies
it immediately made English spelling match the way words were pronounced
it introduced French spellings into English for the first time ever
questions.explanation: Print reproduced the same forms across thousands of copies, so particular spellings became familiar and fixed. Spelling did not come to match pronunciation; the gap widened as pronunciation kept changing.

questions.stem: Words such as ‘knight’ and ‘knee’ keep a ‘k’ that is no longer pronounced. The main reason is that:
options: Johnson added the ‘k’ to show that the words came from Latin
the ‘k’ was never pronounced at any stage in Old English
American printers inserted the letter to regularise spelling
spelling was fixed in print while pronunciation kept changing
questions.explanation: The /k/ was pronounced in Old and Middle English and was lost from speech after spellings had been settled by print. These are native Germanic words, so a Latin origin cannot explain the letter.

questions.stem: The ‘b’ in ‘debt’, a word borrowed from French ‘dette’, has never been pronounced in English. It was added by Renaissance scholars to:
options: reflect the word's origin in Latin ‘debitum’
mark a long vowel after the Great Vowel Shift
separate it from its Old Norse cognate
show that the word came from Norman French
questions.explanation: Writers in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries respelt some words to display their Latin roots, so ‘dette’ became ‘debt’ and ‘doute’ became ‘doubt’. The French spelling had no ‘b’, so the letter does not show a French origin.

questions.stem: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language (1755) is important in the codification of English because it:
options: set out the rules of English grammar that were then taught in schools
replaced Latin as the language of the English law courts
became a widely accepted reference for spelling and meaning
was the first book ever printed in the English language
questions.explanation: Johnson's dictionary gave a large, authoritative record of English words with definitions and quotations, and its spellings became a standard reference. It was a dictionary, not a grammar, so it did not set grammatical rules.

questions.stem: American spellings such as ‘color’ and ‘center’ are largely the result of:
questions.explanation: Webster's American dictionary of 1828 promoted simplified spellings to mark a distinct American standard. Johnson's dictionary kept ‘colour’ and ‘centre’, which Australian English still follows.

questions.stem: Initialisms such as ‘brb’ and ‘tbh’ spread quickly as a result of which development?
questions.explanation: Fast, informal written exchanges on phones and online encouraged abbreviated forms that save keystrokes. These are written conventions of computer-mediated communication, far later than print or dictionaries.

questions.stem: When the Macquarie Dictionary adds a word because it has become widely used, rather than because it is considered correct, it is taking:
options: a universal grammar approach to language
questions.explanation: Descriptivism records how language is actually used. A prescriptivist dictionary would include only the forms its editors judged correct, regardless of how widely others were used.

questions.stem: English belongs to which branch of the Indo-European language family?
questions.explanation: English is a West Germanic language, closely related to Frisian, Dutch and German. Its large French and Latin vocabulary is borrowed, which does not make it a Romance language.

questions.stem: English ‘father’, German ‘Vater’, Latin ‘pater’ and Ancient Greek ‘patēr’ resemble each other because they:
options: were all borrowed from Latin by the other languages
imitate a sound, so they are onomatopoeic words
spread from English to Europe through trade
descend from a common ancestor, Proto-Indo-European
questions.explanation: These words are cognates, inherited from a shared ancestor language rather than borrowed. English ‘father’ is a native Germanic word, not a borrowing from Latin.

questions.stem: English is a Germanic language, yet a large share of its dictionary vocabulary comes from French and Latin. Why is it still classed as Germanic?
options: its core grammar and most frequent words descend from Germanic
most of the words in an English dictionary are Germanic in origin
English borrowed no French or Latin words before about 1500
linguists classify every language by the alphabet it is written in
questions.explanation: Languages are classified by descent, and the basic words (‘the’, ‘and’, ‘water’, ‘house’) and grammar of English come from Old English. Borrowed words are numerous in the dictionary, but they do not change a language's family.

questions.stem: Latin ‘pes’ matches English ‘foot’, and Latin ‘piscis’ matches English ‘fish’. These regular p-to-f correspondences show that:
options: the words are unrelated and their likeness is a coincidence
a regular sound change affected the Germanic branch
English borrowed these words from Latin and simplified them
Latin borrowed the words from Old English and changed them
questions.explanation: Grimm's Law describes systematic consonant changes in early Germanic, including Indo-European p becoming f. The pattern is too regular for coincidence, and ‘foot’ and ‘fish’ are inherited, not borrowed.

questions.stem: The Great Vowel Shift was a change mainly in:
options: the word order of English clauses
questions.explanation: Between the late Middle Ages and the early modern period, most long vowels were raised, and the highest became diphthongs. It changed pronunciation, while spellings stayed largely as they were.

questions.stem: Before the Great Vowel Shift, ‘mouse’ sounded like modern ‘moose’ and ‘shine’ like modern ‘sheen’. What happened to these vowels?
questions.explanation: The close long vowels could not rise further, so they became diphthongs, giving modern ‘mouse’ and ‘shine’. They did not shorten: they are still long sounds, now with a glide.

questions.stem: The letters in ‘name’ and ‘five’ represent quite different vowels in English from those they stand for in most other European languages. The main reason is that:
options: Old Norse speakers changed the vowels of English words
spellings were largely fixed before the Great Vowel Shift ended
English borrowed these spellings from French after 1066
Johnson respelt the words to match their pronunciation
questions.explanation: The vowels in these words shifted after their spellings had settled, so English kept older spellings for new sounds. Johnson recorded existing spellings; he did not respell words to match speech.

questions.stem: ‘Brunch’, formed from ‘breakfast’ and ‘lunch’, is an example of:
questions.explanation: A blend joins parts of two words into one. A compound joins two whole words, as in ‘sunscreen’.

questions.stem: The verb ‘edit’ was formed from the older noun ‘editor’ by removing what looked like a suffix. This process is:
questions.explanation: Backformation removes an apparent affix to make a new word, often of a new class. Conversion changes word class without changing the form at all, as in ‘to text’.

questions.stem: ‘Qantas’ comes from ‘Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services’ and is pronounced as a word. It is:
questions.explanation: An acronym is formed from initial letters and pronounced as a word. An initialism such as ‘ATM’ is pronounced letter by letter.

questions.stem: ‘Flu’ from ‘influenza’ and ‘bus’ from ‘omnibus’ are examples of:
questions.explanation: Shortening (clipping) cuts a longer word down to a part of it, with the same meaning. A contraction such as ‘can’t’ fuses words and marks the missing letters with an apostrophe.

questions.stem: Why is ‘smog’ a blend while ‘sunscreen’ is a compound?
options: ‘smog’ joins parts of two words; ‘sunscreen’ joins two whole words
‘smog’ joins two whole words; ‘sunscreen’ joins two parts of words
‘smog’ is pronounced as letters; ‘sunscreen’ is said as a word
‘smog’ was borrowed from French; ‘sunscreen’ is an Old English word
questions.explanation: ‘Smog’ takes the start of ‘smoke’ and the end of ‘fog’, while ‘sunscreen’ keeps both ‘sun’ and ‘screen’ whole. That difference is what separates blending from compounding.

questions.stem: In ‘I’ll text you later’, the noun ‘text’ is used as a verb without any change of form. This is:
questions.explanation: Conversion changes a word's class with no added affix. Backformation also creates a verb, but only by removing part of an existing word.

questions.stem: ‘Kindergarten’ from German, ‘tsunami’ from Japanese and ‘yoghurt’ from Turkish are examples of:
questions.explanation: Borrowings are words taken from another language into English. A neologism is any newly formed word, which these were not; they already existed in their source languages.

questions.stem: ‘Esky’, ‘thermos’ and ‘velcro’ began as trade names and are now used for any product of that kind. This process is:
questions.explanation: Commonisation turns a brand or proper name into a common noun. The words were not taken from another language, so they are not borrowings.

questions.stem: ‘Thou’ is still found in some religious texts and set phrases but not in everyday speech. It is best described as:
questions.explanation: An archaism is an old form kept only in restricted contexts. An obsolete word has fallen out of use altogether, but ‘thou’ still appears in some texts.

questions.stem: When a word falls out of use, often because the thing it names is no longer common, the process is called:
questions.explanation: Obsolescence is a word gradually disappearing from use, as can happen with names for outdated technology. Narrowing changes a word's meaning but the word stays in use.

questions.stem: As English lost most of its noun case endings in the Middle English period, it came to rely more heavily on:
options: rising intonation to mark the object of a verb
fixed word order to show who did what to whom
prefixes added to verbs to mark the subject
questions.explanation: In Old English, case endings showed a noun's role, so word order was more flexible. Once the endings were lost, the subject–verb–object order became the main signal of grammatical roles.

questions.stem: Early Modern English ‘Know you not the cause?’ would now be ‘Don’t you know the cause?’ This change shows:
options: the rise of ‘do’ as an auxiliary in questions and negatives
a shift from subject–verb–object to subject–object–verb
the loss of the second-person pronoun ‘you’ from English
semantic narrowing of the verb ‘know’ since Shakespeare
questions.explanation: Earlier English could invert a lexical verb with its subject and place ‘not’ after it; Modern English uses the auxiliary ‘do’ for this. ‘You’ appears in both versions, so no pronoun has been lost.

questions.stem: ‘Holiday’ once meant only a religious feast day, a ‘holy day’, but now means any day off. This semantic change is:
questions.explanation: The word now covers a wider range of meanings than before, which is broadening. Narrowing would be the reverse: a general meaning becoming more specific.

questions.stem: ‘Meat’ once meant food of any kind, as in ‘meat and drink’, but now usually means animal flesh. This semantic change is:
questions.explanation: A general meaning has become more specific, which is narrowing. The older sense survives only in fixed phrases such as ‘one man's meat is another man's poison’.

questions.stem: ‘Knight’ comes from an Old English word meaning ‘boy’ or ‘servant’, but came to mean a noble mounted warrior. This semantic change is:
questions.explanation: The word moved from naming a low-status person to a high-status one, which is elevation (amelioration). Deterioration would move the meaning downwards.

questions.stem: ‘Bird’ comes from Old English ‘bridd’ (a young bird), and ‘deer’ from Old English ‘dēor’ (any animal). Which semantic changes do these words show, respectively?
questions.explanation: ‘Bird’ widened from a young bird to any bird, while ‘deer’ narrowed from any animal to one kind. Reversing the two is the common slip.

questions.stem: ‘Bead’ comes from an Old English word meaning ‘prayer’. Because prayers were counted on rosary beads, it came to mean the small ball itself. This is best described as:
questions.explanation: The meaning has moved to a different but associated referent, from the prayer to the object used to count it, which is shift. The new meaning is neither a wider nor a narrower version of ‘prayer’.

questions.stem: Prescriptivism is an approach to language that:
options: records how language is actually used
explains how young children acquire their first language
traces the origins of individual words
sets out rules for how language should be used
questions.explanation: Prescriptivists focus on correctness and preserving an ideal standard. Recording actual use is descriptivism, and tracing word origins is etymology.

questions.stem: A letter to a newspaper complains that people now use ‘literally’ for emphasis, as in ‘I literally died laughing’, and says this proves standards are falling. This view is:
questions.explanation: Treating change as decline and one use as the only correct one is a prescriptivist attitude. A descriptivist would note that the intensifying use is widespread and describe it.

questions.stem: Some people write ‘could of’ for ‘could have’. Which response is most consistent with a descriptivist approach?
options: argue that dictionaries should refuse to list any non-standard spelling
treat it as clear evidence that young people today cannot think clearly
record who writes it and explain that it comes from the spoken ‘could’ve’
insist on correcting it, because ‘could have’ is the only acceptable form
questions.explanation: A descriptivist observes and explains usage: in speech ‘’ve’ sounds like ‘of’, which accounts for the spelling. Insisting on correction is prescriptivist, whatever the merits of the standard form in formal writing.
